#6477. The 8 Best Cordless Stick Vacuums Are Convenient, Versatile, and Work Well on Carpets Too

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

When testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

Its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

The auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

This cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

It also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

The motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

This cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

The vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

It’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

Beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

This vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#6476. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6469. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6466. A virtual escape may help children feel less scared before surgery

Children reported less fear after brief virtual reality sessions before surgery, offering early evidence for a possible drug-free calming option.

Before an operation, plenty of children are scared, and a common way to calm them is a sedative that carries risks of its own.

Researchers tested a drug-free option: a virtual reality headset showing a calm playroom or a quiet beach.

After a short session in it, children said they felt less upset and less scared, while their heart rates went down.

Whether the headset deserves the credit is still an open question.

Walaa Abu Rukbah, a pharmacist at the University of Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, is the study’s first author.

“Sometimes, the best support we can offer a child before surgery isn’t a medicine at all,” said Abu Rukbah.

The project ran for nine months at a children’s hospital in Virginia. Every child in it used the headset, so there was no group of children who waited without one to compare against.

Between half and three-quarters of children feel anxious before surgery, by the researchers’ estimate.

A scared child isn’t only unhappy. Very anxious children are more likely to struggle when it’s time to go under anesthesia.

They’re also more likely to wake up confused and agitated, a state doctors call emergence delirium, and to have more pain and a slower recovery.

The calming drug used most often is midazolam. It can make some children more agitated instead of calmer, and it can slow breathing or delay the trip home.

Drug-free options such as play therapy and music have helped children in earlier studies, but they need trained staff that not every hospital has.

The team spent 10 months designing its own virtual world for children.

The main scene is a playroom in soft blues and greens, with toys that respond when a child looks at them and slow music in the background.

A second scene shows a beach with waves and palm trees.

Some people experience motion sickness in virtual reality because what they see does not match the motion their body senses.

To avoid that, children hop from spot to spot instead of gliding around. When 15 children tried it early on, none of them reported feeling sick.

From October 2023 to June 2024, 80 children aged 6 to 15 used the headset while waiting for planned surgery at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU.

Their parents could watch on a tablet what the child was seeing. A typical session lasted about nine minutes, though some ran as long as 20.

Before and after each session, children rated how upset they felt from 0 to 10, much like the pain scales doctors use.

They also pointed to one of five faces, ranging from calm to very scared.

The typical child’s score dropped from 3 to 1 on the 0-to-10 scale. On the faces, the typical child pointed to the second face before the session and the calmest face after it.

Not every child changed much. By the team’s measure of a change big enough to matter, 46 of the 80 children felt noticeably less upset afterward and 44 felt noticeably less scared. That’s a little more than half.

Bedside monitors picked up a change too. Heart rate dropped by nearly six beats a minute on average.

Systolic blood pressure – the top number in a blood pressure reading – fell by about 4 points on average.

Only three children had any side effects, and all of them were minor.

Dayanjan Wijesinghe, a researcher in the Department of Pharmacotherapy and Outcomes Science at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), was also involved in the study.

“In a busy children’s surgical unit, a short virtual reality session proved easy for nurses to run, was safe, and was very popular: nine in ten children wanted to use it again, and nearly every parent would recommend it,” said Wijesinghe.

All 29 nurses involved said they would recommend it too.

When parents wrote about the experience, they mentioned distraction more than anything else.

“He was distracted and didn’t notice when the needle went in,” one parent wrote.

Not every parent was equally enthusiastic.

“If my child chose it, sure. To me it’s a bit overwhelming to have so much going on,” another parent wrote.

Waiting rooms can get easier on their own. A child might calm down simply from getting used to the room, or from having an adult pay close attention for a while.

The most scared children had the biggest drops.

However, unusually high initial scores can fall on a second measurement even without an effective treatment, potentially making the headset appear more helpful.

Scientists call this regression to the mean, and it can make health programs look better than they really are.

The team’s own checks suggested it explains much of why the most anxious children improved the most.

Families also knew they were trying something new, and the study team collected their ratings in person. That can lead people to give kinder answers.

Once the children left the waiting room, the researchers stopped tracking them.

Whether a calmer wait leads to an easier start to anesthesia or a faster recovery wasn’t measured.

All of the children came from a single hospital, so a hospital with different staff or patients might see different results.

In the researchers’ view, the next step is a randomized trial that compares the headset with usual care and with other drug-free options.

Such a trial could also show whether a headset costs less than giving children a sedative.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Digital Health.

#6465. California schools must drop ultra-processed food, and kitchen managers explain why that’s hard

California will phase ultra-processed foods out of school meals, but kitchen directors say money, staff and small kitchens stand in the way.

Taking junk food off school menus sounds like a matter of writing a rule. California has written one, and starting in 2029 its schools must begin phasing out many ultra-processed foods.

But when researchers asked the people who run school kitchens what makes cooking from scratch hard, the answers were money, staff and kitchens built mostly to reheat.

Many districts even buy basic ingredients, then pay to have them turned into the processed foods that the law targets.

That’s the gap between a law and a lunch line, and the directors said closing it will take more than a deadline.

The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act requires California schools to begin phasing out certain ultra-processed foods in July 2029 and finish by 2035. These are factory-made foods with ingredients that home cooks rarely use, such as flavorings, colorings and emulsifiers.

Such foods make up about two-thirds of the calories U.S. children eat, according to studies the authors cite. School meals can supply about half of a child’s daily calories, which makes the cafeteria a big lever on what kids eat.

Andrea Pedroza-Tobias, then an instructor at Stanford Medicine and now at UC Irvine, led the study with pediatrician Anisha Patel.

Community groups, including the Dolores Huerta Foundation and Cultiva La Salud, helped shape it, along with the Nutrition Policy Institute at the University of California.

From January to June 2024, the team interviewed food service directors from 20 school districts in California’s San Joaquin Valley, a farming region with many low-income families.

The districts were picked at random from urban and rural areas, and from districts with and without a state grant for freshly prepared meals.

Sixteen of the directors also filled out a short survey. On average, their districts served some scratch-cooked items about 2.5 days a week and heat-and-serve foods about 3 days a week.

That is a small group in one region. The authors note that the results may not match other parts of the country, and that directors who agreed to talk may care more about scratch cooking than those who didn’t.

Two-thirds of the surveyed directors identified staff shortages and a lack of money for labor as obstacles. Many rely on part-time workers who can reheat food but don’t have time to cook it. Storage and kitchen space came next.

State grants for kitchen equipment helped, but the money went different ways. Some districts bought skillets and ranges for cooking, while others bought more ovens to assist with reheating. Directors also said one-year grants made it hard to plan for the long run.

Most did credit California’s free meals for every student with bringing in more money, and in some districts more cooks.

In an interview with Earth.com, Patel and Pedroza-Tobias said the money has to come with guidelines for using it. “However, funding alone is not enough,” they said. They pointed to policies, practices and technical assistance paired with funding.

Schools get raw ingredients through a federal food program, but many districts ship them out to be processed. “I’m sending my chicken to, let’s say, Tyson and getting chicken patties and chicken nuggets,” one director told the researchers.

Directors also said most products labeled and sold for schools, the ones built to meet federal nutrition rules, are ultra-processed.

Amanda Harvey, who runs nutrition services for Fresno Unified and sat on the study’s advisory board, has seen supply problems firsthand. When her district dropped products with food dye, pickles made without green dye became hard to find.

“They’re pricey for pickles, and it can be quite challenging for our vendor to get them,” Harvey said. Another director recalled spending years removing cooking equipment and buying more processed food, and now using grant money to buy the same kinds of kettles and skillets back.

Some directors worried students would skip scratch-cooked meals and throw more food away. Others said students preferred fresh, familiar food, and they described ways to win kids over, including taste tests, family nutrition nights and student recipe contests.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised them most, the researchers pointed to districts that found creative ways around tight budgets. “One food service director even dressed in costumes to encourage children to try healthier foods,” they said.

They also noted that at least seven other states have passed laws on specific food additives or dyes, though most still allow some ultra-processed foods. Brazil’s national school meal program, they said, requires at least 85 percent of federal food funds to go to fresh or minimally processed foods.

The directors described what they expect and what they’ve tried. The study didn’t measure what children actually ate, how their health changed, or whether the new law’s timeline is realistic.

The authors call for money to hire and keep staff, upgrade kitchens and train cooks, along with rules that make ultra-processed products less attractive to buy.

Whether California’s districts can make that switch by 2035 will show up on real trays over the next decade, and no one has measured it yet.

Research on kids’ behavior and toddler foods has kept attention on processed food in childhood, and on its health risks. Schools may be where the change is easiest to track.

The full study was published in the journal Public Health Nutrition.

#6464. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6462. How does a flavor become a favorite? Scientists uncover a gut-brain signal

A slow dopamine signal helps mice learn to prefer flavors linked to calories, offering clues to how food preferences develop.

Coffee can be a hard sell on the first sip. It’s bitter, and people naturally tend to avoid bitter tastes, yet many grow to love it.

A new study offers a clue to how we acquire food preferences over time.

Working mainly with mice, scientists found a slow dopamine signal that helps the brain connect a flavor with calories arriving in the gut.

The signal reaches a small part of the amygdala, and human brain scans pointed to a similar spot.

James Grove, then a graduate student at UC San Francisco, ran most of the experiments in the lab of senior author Zachary Knight, a UCSF physiology professor.

“We’ve shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens,” Knight said.

When we eat, taste and calories usually come together.

The researchers needed to separate them to see which one prompted the brain to release dopamine, a chemical messenger.

They fitted mice with a thin tube through the stomach wall and delivered sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid directly into the stomach.

About a fifth of a teaspoon went in over 10 minutes while sensors tracked dopamine in four brain regions.

Two regions that feature heavily in reward research, the nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum, showed no response to the nutrients.

That matched an earlier experiment from Knight’s lab.

Instead, dopamine rose in the front of the basolateral amygdala. In mice, this structure measures only about a tenth of an inch (2.5 mm) from front to back.

The back half of the basolateral amygdala did not respond to nutrients. It did respond to a drug that made mice feel sick.

The front section’s signal also followed a different timetable from dopamine released in response to taste.

Taste signals come and go within seconds, but this one began about 48 seconds after nutrients entered the stomach.

It stayed high for about nine minutes after the infusion ended. That gave the researchers a way to distinguish the slower response to nutrients from the quick response to flavor.

Next, mice drank two saccharin-sweetened solutions, one lemon-lime and one grape. Licking one triggered glucose delivery into the stomach, while licking the other delivered plain water.

After six days, mice with normal dopamine activity strongly favored the flavor paired with glucose. Its share of their licks rose from about 35% to 81%.

When researchers used light to switch off dopamine-producing cells in the midbrain during training, the mice showed little change in preference.

The glucose-paired flavor’s share of their licks rose only from 48% to 53%.

These mice kept drinking, although they drank less of the newly paired flavor on the first day.

The experiment included roughly equal numbers of males and females. Both showed similar dopamine responses.

Turning off dopamine neurons didn’t stop every kind of learning. Mice that tried a new flavor and then received lithium chloride, which causes nausea, still learned to avoid it.

So the mice could still learn that a flavor made them feel ill. Learning to like a flavor because it came with nutrition depended on a different brain system.

The team then offered mice two calorie-free flavors and used light to activate dopamine fibers in the front of the amygdala 20 seconds after they licked one of them.

The mice learned to prefer that flavor even though no nutrients arrived.

The same stimulation in the nucleus accumbens, dorsal striatum, central amygdala, or back of the basolateral amygdala did not create a preference.

In the dorsal striatum, it had the opposite effect: the paired flavor’s share of licks fell from about 61% to 37%.

Stimulating the fibers in the front of the basolateral amygdala did not change how much the mice ate.

The mice also wouldn’t press a lever just to get that stimulation.

Unlike many dopamine signals, this one didn’t seem rewarding by itself, but pairing it with a flavor taught a lasting preference.

The gut’s response to sugar depended on SGLT1, a protein that transports certain sugars across the intestinal wall.

Sugars that activated it prompted dopamine release, while fructose and mannitol did not.

A drug that blocked SGLT1 stopped the response. Fat used a different set of sensors, and blocking three of them stopped the dopamine response to fat.

Other research has also found separate gut pathways for sugar and fat.

Using a microscope, the team watched individual amygdala neurons as mice drank. About 58% became active when the mice licked sucrose, beginning as soon as licking started.

The same cells responded to sucralose, a sweetener with no calories. But that response faded during a single session, while the response to sucrose held steady.

Sweet taste and signals from the gut reached the same cells, which kept responding when the sweetness came with calories.

Silencing those cells during training stopped the mice from learning a preference without stopping them from eating.

Until then, the researchers had recorded only the brain’s left hemisphere.

When they checked both sides in the same mice, nutrients raised the dopamine signal by about 18% on the left and about 5% on the right.

Activity at rest was similar on both sides. The difference appeared when nutrients arrived.

Human scans offered a similar clue: Dana Small at Yale reanalyzed a PET study of 13 men who drank a milkshake or a tasteless drink.

Dopamine release after the drink reached the stomach was concentrated in the left front amygdala.

Marc Tittgemeyer and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Metabolism Research in Cologne scanned 38 adults after a glucose drink. Activity increased in the same left-side area.

In mice, cutting the vagus nerve on either side roughly halved the response in both brain hemispheres. That suggested the left-right difference did not come from signals traveling along that nerve.

The team then traced the brain regions feeding into each side of the pathway.

The biggest difference appeared in the visceral cortex, part of the insula that processes signals from inside the body.

Scientists generally expect circuits for basic tasks such as feeding to work similarly on both sides of the brain.

Knight’s lab is now studying the connections between the insula and amygdala to understand why this signal is stronger on the left.

The human evidence is more limited, and scans after a drink cannot show that this signal teaches people to prefer a flavor.

Unlike the mouse experiments, the human studies did not deliver nutrients straight into the stomach and measure the dopamine response that followed.

The study also did not test GLP-1 drugs. Knight suspects they might reduce dopamine release in response to nutrients, making food less reinforcing over time, but that possibility remains untested.

“By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods,” Knight said.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6461. Why do the faintest galaxies around the Milky Way all hold about the same amount of iron?

Simulations suggest the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way share one iron level because a single giant first star exploded in each.

Smaller galaxies usually hold less iron, so the faintest ones circling the Milky Way should be the poorest of all. They aren’t. Below a certain size, they all carry about the same small share of iron, and computer models have struggled for years to explain why.

New simulations suggest an answer. In most of these tiny galaxies, the iron came from a single explosion of one giant star from the Universe’s first generation.

The simulations come from MEGATRON, a project led by Martin Rey of the University of Bath with collaborators at the University of Chicago and the Institut d’Astrophysique de Paris (IAP).

They’re computer models rather than telescope observations, and the result depends on assumptions that remain uncertain about the first stars.

Every carbon, oxygen and iron atom around us was made inside a star, Rey said. The very first stars formed from hydrogen and helium alone, and their explosions started that process.

In an interview with Earth.com, Rey explained why the oldest surviving stars matter. “Those old stars are basically a fossil record, preserving the chemical fingerprints of events that happened over 13 billion years ago,” he said.

Many of those stars belong to ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, the dimmest galaxies orbiting the Milky Way. Each holds no more than about 100,000 times the Sun’s mass in stars. They stopped making new stars long ago, so astronomers treat them as relics of the early universe.

Among larger dwarf galaxies, iron drops as size drops. For the smallest ones, however, that trend flattens out. Their stars average roughly one three-hundredth of the Sun’s share of iron, and astronomers call this the iron plateau.

Earlier simulations had trouble giving such small galaxies that much iron.

The MEGATRON team simulated a patch of the early Universe that will grow into a galaxy with the Milky Way’s mass. The program follows gas, starlight and chemistry at once, keeping count of more than 80 kinds of atoms and molecules.

That matters because the project aims to connect two views of the early Universe. The James Webb Space Telescope sees young galaxies directly, while old stars nearby keep a chemical record of the same era.

Four versions started from the same point. Each used different assumptions about the second generation of stars, which formed after the first stars had added heavier elements to the gas. All four used the same recipe for the first stars.

Together, the runs produced more than 500 small galaxies. They end about 12 billion years before the present.

In all four versions, most of the smallest galaxies ended up with the iron level astronomers measure in real ones. About 78 percent fell inside the plateau’s range, between a thousandth and a hundredth of the Sun’s share.

Since only the second-generation recipe changed between runs, the authors took that as a sign that the first stars set the pattern.

Most of the small galaxies had exactly one first-generation star explode inside them. Those on the plateau mostly got their iron from stars, between 160 and 300 times the Sun’s mass, which blow themselves apart.

Each of those explosions makes about five times the Sun’s mass in iron, according to the published estimates the team used.

Asked what surprised him most, Rey told Earth.com, “In our simulations, this plateau falls out naturally from the physics of the first stars.” The team hadn’t gone looking for it.

“The simulations were never designed to reproduce it and we had not even planned to explore or look into this question,” he said. One of his collaborators suggested making the figure out of curiosity.

An explosion that powerful can blast its debris out of a small galaxy. In MEGATRON, that mostly didn’t happen.

Ultraviolet light from the young central galaxy kept gas from forming the hydrogen molecules it needs to cool down and collapse into stars. So the first stars couldn’t form in the smallest clumps of matter.

They formed instead in heavier clumps of dark matter and gas, about 10 million times the Sun’s mass, with enough gravity to hold on to the debris. Later stars then formed from that iron-enriched gas.

The authors checked this with a simple calculation. Spreading five Suns’ worth of iron through the gas in one of those clumps matches the plateau’s average level.

A lighter giant star, around 140 times the Sun’s mass, makes about a tenth as much iron, which leaves its galaxy well below the plateau.

About 22 percent of the small simulated galaxies fall below the plateau, with less than a thousandth of the Sun’s share of iron. No ultra-faint galaxy measured so far is that poor.

If a fifth of them really were, the chance of finding none among the 38 measured would be about 0.02 percent, the authors calculated. That counts against the prediction.

Still, the census is thin. Many of these galaxies have iron measured in only a few stars. One of them, Pictor II, averages right at the plateau’s lower edge, and it holds a star with almost no iron.

Both groups would still exist today, according to the team’s forecast. Most small galaxies get torn apart and spread into the faint cloud of stars around a galaxy like the Milky Way, called the halo.

In a companion study led by Anatole Storck, the team found that 75 to 80 percent of the first stars’ remains end up there, Rey said.

“So the debris of the very first generation of stars is, quite literally, still out there around us,” Rey said.

MEGATRON’s plateau rests on three assumptions, and the authors wrote that each is uncertain. Ultraviolet light from the young galaxy has to be strong. The first stars have to be mostly giants. And each giant explosion has to make a lot of iron.

That second assumption is debated, since some newer models suggest the first stars were lighter. The simulations also make much less nitrogen than astronomers measure in real old stars, and the simulated young galaxy may not match the Milky Way’s early history.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is expected to find many new faint galaxies, and the next generation of very large telescopes should measure the iron in their stars.

Rey has been awarded 40 million hours of processing time on the U.K.’s national supercomputers for the next round. He compared that to running five million laptops for a year.

With them, his team will test “which assumptions about the first stars match local data, and more importantly which do not,” he said.

One galaxy found below the plateau would fit the prediction. If surveys keep finding none, the first stars may have been even heavier than assumed, or the plateau has another cause.

The full study was published in the journal The Open Journal of Astrophysics.
