#6448. Decades of research show just how much wild animals depend on insects for food, shelter and medicine

Moths feed algae in sloth fur, parrots live in termite mounds, and ants arm poison frogs. So, insect decline is costing wildlife more than just meals.

Brown-throated sloths carry moths in their fur, and the moths help feed them. The insects leave nitrogen behind, which feeds algae growing in the fur, and the sloths eat the algae.

Once a month, a sloth climbs down to the forest floor to leave its droppings, and the moths lay their eggs in them.

A new review of hundreds of studies finds partnerships like this all over the animal world. Animals with backbones, from bats to frogs, depend on insects for shelter, protection and cleanup, not only for meals.

When insects decline, the authors conclude, many of those animals are likely to suffer.

Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, led the work.

She shared the lead with Rob Cooke of the U.K. Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) and Chris Elphick of the University of Connecticut. Members of the team spanned eight countries.

It’s a review, so they gathered decades of other scientists’ findings rather than collecting new field data.

“We often hear about their importance as pollinators, or decomposers, or food for insectivores like birds and bats, but we forget about all the other things they do for us and for other species,” Grames said.

Food is the best-documented link. The team pulled together diet records for 19,750 species of land and freshwater animals with backbones, about two in five of all such species.

Of those, 73 percent eat insects or other invertebrates, meaning animals without a backbone, such as spiders and worms, and 44 percent eat nothing else.

Those records are lopsided. Diets are on file for 95 percent of bird species, but for only 4 percent of ray-finned fish species.

Birds need insects most when they breed. Of North America’s land birds, 96 percent raise their chicks partly or entirely on insects. Purple martins alone eat an estimated 412 billion insects a year.

Other animals binge. A Couch’s spadefoot toad can eat more than half its body weight in termites at a single feeding, enough calories to last it a year. Diets built on ants and termites have evolved again and again.

Some animals use insects to get other food. Certain herons and egrets set insects on the water’s surface to lure fish. Kangaroo rats raid lines of harvester ants and steal the seeds the ants are carrying.

Termite mounds and ant nests tend to hold steady temperatures and are well ventilated, which makes them good shelters. Small mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians all use termite mounds when they breed.

Hooded parrots live inside them. White-throated round-eared bats dig out and maintain cavities in termite mounds, using a kind of scent camouflage to fend off attacks.

Frogs, salamanders and reptiles use ant nests to escape predators. Some also move in during dry seasons, because the humidity inside stays steady.

Some frogs, lizards and snakes lay their eggs in ant nests, and in some cases fungus-growing ants groom the eggs and cover them with material from their fungus gardens.

Other animals reuse what insects leave behind. Some bats move into abandoned holes made by longhorn beetle larvae.

Many birds use spider and insect silk in their nests, which strengthens them, keeps them warm and helps hide them. Bowerbirds decorate the structures they build to attract mates with butterfly wings and beetle parts.

Living near stinging insects can pay off. Many small birds build their nests close to wasps, ants or other stinging insects, and experiments suggest that choice helps more nests succeed.

Other animals take the insects’ chemical weapons for themselves. Pitohui birds carry toxins that come from the melyrid beetles they eat, and those toxins likely deter ticks and predators. Some snakes eat firefly larvae and store the toxins.

Amphibians probably do it more than any other group. Scientists have detected more than 800 defensive chemicals in amphibian skin, and most of them come from insects in the diet.

In some toxic poison frogs, ants make up 50 to 73 percent of what they eat, while ants are a much smaller part of the diet for their harmless relatives.

That means a frog’s chemical defenses depend partly on which insects are around to eat. When the available prey changes, the mix of toxins in its skin can change too.

Chimpanzees apply insects to open wounds, though scientists don’t know which chemicals are involved or what the treatment does.

More than 200 bird species use ants to groom themselves, a habit called anting. Proposed reasons include removing parasites, easing skin irritation and keeping feathers in good shape.

Insects also clean up. In hooded parrot nests, a moth lives alongside the chicks and eats their droppings. Moths in owl and kingfisher nests break down fur, crushed feathers and leftover pellets.

The arrangement is old: a beetle was feeding on shed feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period.

Dung beetles help on a bigger scale. By drying out dung and letting air into it, they leave fewer parasites alive inside.

Where antiparasitic drugs, such as ivermectin, are given to livestock dung beetle communities have been devastated, and much less dung gets removed. What that means for disease in wild animals isn’t well studied.

The relationship isn’t all help. Mosquitoes spread avian malaria, which affects bird species worldwide, and mantids occasionally catch hummingbirds.

Researchers studying insect losses have mostly asked what happens to the food supply, and some of the numbers are stark.

Across Europe, insect-eating birds declined by 13 percent from 1990 to 2015, while birds with mixed diets held steady. Of the 3 billion birds North America has lost since 1970, 2.9 billion came from species that rely on insects for at least part of their lives.

That doesn’t prove the insects caused it. Bird, bat and insect declines don’t always line up on a map, and they may be separate responses to the same environmental pressures.

A pooled analysis of 125 studies did link more insect prey to birds raising more young, with chicks in better condition.

The risk is sharper for picky eaters like the Critically Endangered mountain pygmy possum, which times its breeding around the bogong moth. After the moth’s steep decline over the past decade, the possum’s shrinking food supply is now a primary threat.

The extinction of the Eskimo curlew has been blamed in part on the loss of the Rocky Mountain locust, a large part of its diet. “If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

The team checked its diet records against the IUCN Red List, the global record of species at risk. Of the 622 Critically Endangered species in those records, 202 eat only invertebrates, so their survival depends on having enough of them.

Yet the Red List assessments for those species say little about insect decline as a main cause. Most threatened species lack detailed diet records, and losing food is tangled up with losing habitat.

Most insect species haven’t been formally described. Many diet studies lump insects together with spiders, worms and other invertebrates. And experiments that start with the insects and follow the effects up to the animals that eat them are lacking.

The review came out of the Status of Insects research network. The authors call for shared standards for recording which insects animals eat and use.

They also favor closer work between researchers who study animals with backbones and those who are insect specialists. Citizen science photos and DNA traces from the environment could also help.

Until that data exists, researchers can’t reliably rank which of these thousands of partnerships animals can least afford to lose.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Reviews Biodiversity.

#6447. ALS Stole His Voice—Then, a ‘Digital Twin’ Read His Thoughts And Started Speaking for Him

This technology could restore the art of conversation for people with paralysis, but questions remain about who is really in control.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Did Walter want coffee? His virtual avatar responded, but it gave an unexpected answer. Instead of nodding or signaling yes with a thumbs-up, it waved goodbye. The mistake was funny, but it illustrated a serious problem: When technology communicates on someone’s behalf, an incorrect gesture can change the meaning of an entire exchange.

Walter, who has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, knows how much can be lost when communication becomes difficult. He went from slightly slurred speech to being unintelligible within approximately six months. He eventually relied on emails, text-to-speech applications, and telephone relay services. ALS is a progressive neurological disease that damages the nerve cells responsible for voluntary muscle movement, gradually affecting a person’s ability to speak, swallow, move, and breathe. Although the disease weakens muscles, it does not necessarily impair thinking or understanding.

“Somehow you try to keep a communication going while compromising to focus on the most essential content,” Walter says. “That doesn’t leave space for emotions and gestures at all.”

Determined to find a more efficient way to communicate, Walter began researching brain-computer interfaces. After attending an ALS Association webinar about emerging technologies, he discovered that neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, at the University of California, San Francisco, was leading a study that could potentially change lives. He contacted the research team himself, undeterred by the prospect of the invasive implant it would require. With ALS shortening his life expectancy, he also saw participation as an opportunity to advance technology that might benefit future patients, even if he never lived to use a commercial version.

The team began working with Walter on the virtual avatar in early summer 2025, gradually training the system to recognize his attempted speech and movements separately before combining them. “Every step and progress was fascinating and quite unbelievable at the same time,” he recalls. But the defining moment came when the avatar successfully decoded his speech and gestures together. “What a great milestone!” he says.

The research team’s brain-computer interface (BCI) decodes attempted speech and gestures simultaneously through a single implant, translating those signals into words and movements performed by a personalized virtual avatar. Their study, published in Nature Neuroscience, offers a glimpse of technology that could eventually restore something beyond words: the expressive dimensions of human conversation.

The process of getting your own virtual avatar started with electrocorticography (ECoG), which records electrical activity from electrodes positioned over the brain’s surface. The researchers’ implant covered a broad region of the sensorimotor cortex, which is involved in controlling speech and movement. Different areas are more strongly associated with different body movements, providing clues that machine-learning models can use to distinguish attempted speech from gestures.

But the researchers encountered an unexpected complication.

“What surprised us was that models trained on speech and gestures separately didn’t work as well when participants attempted both at the same time,” Samantha Brosler, a UCSF researcher and first co-author of the study, says.

The problem involved overlapping neural activity. Some brain regions respond during both speech and gesture attempts, and their activity patterns can change when those actions occur together.

Jennifer Collinger, PhD, a neuroprosthetics researcher at the University of Pittsburgh who was not involved in the research, describes this as context-dependent neural activity. “The neural activity associated with a particular movement, such as waving, may be different depending on whether or not you are speaking at the same time,” she explains.

To address this, the UCSF team, led by neurosurgeon Edward Chang, MD, trained two parallel decoding models using recordings of participants attempting speech and gestures separately and together. A participant attempting to say “hello” while waving, for example, supplied neural activity that could train one model to recognize the phrase and another to recognize the movement. The combined training improved decoding performance.

Encouragingly, the models could recognize some speech-and-gesture combinations they had not encountered during training. That matters because teaching a system every possible combination of human words and movements would be impractical.

The study involved three participants with paralysis, although the main simultaneous speech-and-gesture experiments involved two. For a participant with ALS, the researchers tested 10 predefined phrases and 10 gestures. For one participant, the system recognized 10 conversational phrases, including “hello,” “thank you,” “nice to meet you,” and “how’s it going?,” alongside 10 gestures such as waving, nodding, shrugging, pointing, and shaking hands. The avatar could combine the two, allowing someone to say “hello” while waving or “nice to meet you” while extending a hand. Researchers tested all 100 possible phrase-and-gesture pairings, including combinations that would rarely occur in ordinary conversation, to assess how reliably the system could decode both actions together. During real-time testing, speech decoding reached 70 percent accuracy, and gesture decoding reached 66 percent. Offline testing for participants with paralysis following a brainstem stroke also produced valuable results.

Collinger considers the findings encouraging but emphasizes their experimental boundaries, in part because this study was limited to a finite set of speech and gesture actions. The system wasn’t generating spontaneous conversation. It recognized predefined phrases, displayed decoded speech as text, and triggered corresponding avatar animations when gestures were detected.

That distinction raises questions about user control. Walter’s accidental goodbye was amusing, but an incorrect gesture in another situation could misrepresent someone’s intentions. User feedback is essential to ensuring the technology communicates what someone actually intends, Collinger says.

Future versions could allow users to confirm or correct decoded outputs, potentially through eye tracking, Brosler says.

The system currently relies on a wired connection to external computers. An everyday user would need an overhaul that allows true freedom: wireless transmission, portability, and reduced communication delays. It must overcome multiple engineering challenges, Brosler says, such as miniaturizing parts, attaining reliable neural recordings, lowering power consumption, and reducing heat generation.

Walter has his own priorities: the human dimension of the technology’s development. “It’s a two-sided learning curve for the avatar and the patient,” he explains.

An ideal solution would decode a user’s neural cues, he says, adding that wireless mobility and less invasive technology could make such systems more attractive to users.

During one successful experimental dialogue, the system decoded Walter’s attempted speech and gestures together without error. He remembers being overwhelmed. “I was extremely moved by the avatar’s response to my ‘thoughts,’ I couldn’t help laughing uncontrollably with pure joy.”

Even with its limitations, Walter describes the personalized avatar as a digital twin whose movements reflect his intentions and personality.

For Collinger, experiences like Walter’s demonstrate why accuracy alone cannot define success. “Restoring the ability to communicate is not just measured in words per minute,” she says. Independence, relationships, community participation, and personal expression matter, too.

The UCSF experiment has not yet restored unrestricted, natural conversation. But it suggests that the future of brain-computer interfaces may depend on understanding communication as more than the transmission of words—and giving people greater control over everything those words cannot express.

#6446. Dirty air actually breaks down the smell of flowers and stops bees and moths from finding their food

Ozone and nitrogen oxides cut pollinators' ability to find flowers by about half, and ozone will stay high until around 2050 as fuels change.

A bee finds a flower the way you find a bakery, by following the smell. Exhaust from cars and machines breaks those scent molecules apart in the air.

A review of 22 experiments now puts a number on the damage. Polluted air cut how well pollinators found and used flowers by roughly half, and two pollutants together cut it by more than two thirds.

The surprise is in the timing. Even as the world burns less fossil fuel, one of those two pollutants, ozone, isn’t expected to drop below today’s levels until after about 2050.

James Ryalls at the University of Reading led the review with colleagues Jacob Bishop and Carol Wagstaff. In an interview with Earth.com, Ryalls said the result that surprised him most was what the two gases did together.

“It was the first time this interaction had been quantified for pollinators,” he said.

Flowers advertise with chemicals that drift off their petals, and pollinators follow those chemicals to the food. Ozone and nitrogen oxides react with the scent molecules in the air. They break some down and change others, so the trail an insect is following gets weaker and stranger.

Researchers have also linked the gases to duller antennae, poorer learning and memory, and weaker colonies in bees. However, the review ranks that direct damage behind the scent damage.

Ozone is a gas that forms in sunlit air from other pollutants. Nitrogen oxides come mostly from engines, and diesel engines above all.

Ryalls’s team pulled together every experiment it could find that measured flower pollinators in clean air against polluted air. There were 22 studies in all, with 87 comparisons between them.

Most used honeybees or bumblebees. A few used a hawkmoth, a fig wasp or a mix of wild insects, and the setups ranged from lab chambers to greenhouses to open fields with pollutants piped in.

Across those studies, increased ozone lowered pollinator performance by an average of 42 percent, and increased nitrogen oxides lowered it by 46 percent.

Performance here covers three things: how well insect pollinators found flowers, how well they fed on them, and how many turned up.

Only three research teams tested both gases at once, and in those experiments the average loss was 68 percent. That is worse than either gas alone, but well short of the 88 percent you would get by simply adding the two. The gases don’t stack.

Ryalls had an explanation for the gap. “This reflects real atmospheric chemistry, where ozone and nitrogen oxides can partially react with and offset each other,” he told Earth.com.

In the three studies that measured each gas and the pair against the same clean-air control, the extra harm from adding the second gas was smaller still.

The damage was not spread evenly across what insects do. Searching efficiency, the measure of how well a pollinator locates flowers, fell by 67 percent on average. Feeding, once an insect reached a flower, and the number of insects present changed little.

Ryalls said he wanted people to notice that pattern. The insects were not sickened so much as lost.

Specialists have it worst. A bee that visits many kinds of flower can switch cues when one scent breaks down. An insect tied to one plant, like the tobacco hawkmoth or the yucca moth, has no backup.

Timing matters too. Ozone peaks in daylight, when bees and butterflies are out. That is bad timing for crops such as almonds and oilseed rape, whose flowers open in daylight when ozone peaks.

In contrast, nitrogen oxides are often highest at night, when moths do their pollinating. So the two groups face different pollutants, and cutting one gas doesn’t protect both.

Burning less fossil fuel cuts nitrogen oxides. Ozone, however, is made in the air from several ingredients, including methane and carbon monoxide, and those stay high for longer.

Under the middle-of-the-road emissions path used by the IPCC, the authors expect ground-level ozone to stay elevated through mid-century and only drop below today’s levels after about 2050.

On a high-emissions path, ozone is predicted to keep rising into the 2060s. It will only fall below today’s levels near the end of the century.

Diesel vehicles complicate the picture further, because a diesel sold today can stay on the road for more than 20 years. Britain’s decision to push its ban on new gasoline and diesel cars from 2030 to 2035 is the kind of delay the authors said will stretch the hard years out.

One oddity cuts the other way: in cities, nitrogen oxides break down some of the ozone, a buffer that fades in the countryside where there is less exhaust.

“Most of the food we grow depends on healthy pollinators, so protecting them from pollution cannot wait until 2050,” Ryalls said.

Asked by Earth.com what gardeners and farmers can do, Ryalls said cutting local nitrogen oxide emissions would help most.

He suggested replacing older diesel machinery and generators, keeping high-emission equipment idle during peak flowering, expanding green spaces, and letting lawns run wild and flower.

The evidence is lopsided. Of the 22 studies, 19 were done in Europe and 16 used bees or their relatives. That matters because about 70 percent of crop species get some benefit from insect pollination. The countries with the dirtiest air, such as India and China, are the ones likely to be hit hardest.

Flies, beetles and most moths are barely tested, and the tropics, where pollution is often heavier and more insects are generalists, are almost absent from research studies.

The doses were high as well: the average ozone level in the experiments was 161 parts per billion, more than twice the U.S. limit of 70. Harm clearly happened at those levels, but the studies can’t say where it begins.

Whether it starts at a sharp threshold or builds gradually is still an open question, and so is where a safe level might be.

Ryalls wants the next experiments run where the air is already dirty. “I’d like to test these effects in higher-pollution regions and tropical systems, where baseline pollutant levels are often higher and pollinator communities differ,” he said.

His group is also testing treatments that could boost the scents flowers give off, to help insects find them in polluted air.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment.

#6445. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6443. Young children are fascinated by sharks – so why are older kids more fearful?

A survey finds most children like sharks, but older kids express more fear, raising questions about how views of these animals develop.

Sharks have a scary reputation, but many young children like them. Some think they look cool, while others like the way they swim.

A survey of parents of 374 children aged two to 12 found that 69% of the children liked sharks. Older children were more likely to say sharks scared them.

Brianna Le Busque, an environmental psychologist at Adelaide University‘s School of Physics, Chemistry and Earth Sciences, led the study. Parents asked the questions and recorded their children’s answers.

“What’s really interesting is that most of the children in our study actually liked sharks, and many were fascinated by them,” Le Busque said.

People are often less willing to protect animals they fear or dislike. That makes children’s early views of sharks worth understanding.

The few earlier studies on this topic mostly found fear. In a 2020 study, five-year-olds chose a face to show how a shark photo made them feel, and most chose a fearful face.

But those studies left out toddlers. They also usually asked children about sharks alongside other animals, which may have made sharks seem less appealing next to dogs, horses and dolphins.

For the new study, 323 parents took an online survey in 2024. They asked their children what sharks do, what they look like and whether they liked them.

Parents wrote down the answers word for word and noted any hand gestures. They asked brothers and sisters separately so they couldn’t copy each other.

The team counted a child as expressing fear if they called sharks scary, said they were afraid or clearly showed fear another way.

Saying sharks bite or are dangerous didn’t count, because knowing an animal can hurt you doesn’t always mean you fear it.

The most common reason children gave for liking sharks was that they were cool. One four-year-old girl said, “sharks are very cool.”

When describing sharks, 44% mentioned teeth and 33% said they were big. Most talked about sharks swimming and eating, although about one in five said they hurt people.

Some children mixed facts with imagination. A six-year-old boy asked whether sharks were reptiles, then answered himself, “no they’re not, they’re dinosaurs.”

Children who disliked sharks most often said sharks hurt people. One 10-year-old boy explained, “because they could eat me.”

Overall, 13.9% of the children described sharks as scary or expressed fear of them.

Older children did this more often, and the team’s analysis suggested the pattern was unlikely to be due to chance.

“But as children got older, we saw an increase in associations between sharks and fear,” Le Busque said.

“That raises important questions about what children are learning about sharks as they grow up and the role that society, media and other influences might play.”

The team found no clear difference between boys and girls or between children in Australia, the U.S. and the U.K., where most participants lived. How often children went into the ocean made no clear difference either.

The survey compared different age groups. It did not follow the same children as they grew up, so it couldn’t show how any one child’s feelings changed.

Books were the most common way children had come across sharks. About 65% had read shark books or had someone read them aloud.

Another 59% had seen sharks at an aquarium, and 38% had watched TV shows featuring them. About a quarter had seen shark films, including Finding Nemo and Jaws.

Some 13% had sung “Baby Shark,” which became YouTube’s most-viewed video in 2020.

The researchers think these experiences may help explain why many children liked sharks.

Watching sharks swim among other fish at an aquarium, for example, may help children see sharks as more than dangerous animals.

Films may leave a different impression. Older children were more likely to mention Jaws, a film long linked to negative views of sharks and even government responses to shark bites.

Finding Nemo also mixes friendly and frightening images. Bruce appears as a friendly shark trying to stop eating fish, but becomes aggressive when he smells a single drop of blood.

“Sharks are often portrayed in very dramatic and sensational ways, particularly when there is a shark bite or in popular films,” Le Busque said.

Still, the study did not test whether films changed children’s feelings about sharks. The researchers say that needs more study.

Among parents, 44% reported low fear of sharks and 30% reported high fear. Many less fearful parents said they lived far from sharks or could avoid them.

One parent wrote, “The same reason I’m not afraid of earthquakes – I don’t live in an area where they reside.”

The team found no clear link between parents’ fear and their children’s fear.

Some parents said sharks weren’t an everyday threat, which may give children few chances to see their parents react fearfully.

A larger study might find a small link, the researchers noted.

Parents may have influenced their children’s answers or misunderstood them. The researchers accepted that risk because toddlers can’t complete a survey alone.

Views of sharks also differ across cultures, and shark populations vary around the world. Only 14 children in the study were 12, and none were teenagers.

Children’s fear might ease during their teens as they learn more. But strong fears that start in childhood can also last into adulthood.

A recent review found that people who know more about sharks tend to fear them less. Earlier research also linked direct experiences with sharks to greater tolerance of them.

In another study, people who swam with sharks were more likely to report helping sharks two years later.

These findings suggest that learning and positive experiences may help, though they don’t tell us how each child’s feelings will change.

The researchers suggest using lessons and media to show children the many kinds of sharks, helping balance stories built around fear.

“Children are clearly capable of seeing sharks as fascinating, interesting animals, rather than simply something to be afraid of,” Le Busque said.

“Education and positive experiences could be really important in helping children understand sharks as diverse marine animals and appreciate the important role they play in our oceans.”

To learn whether fear fades or lasts, researchers will need to follow the same children into their teens.

They also want future studies to use a standard set of questions about fear, making the results easier to compare.

The study is published in the journal Human Dimensions of Wildlife.

#6442. The 7 Best Robot Vacuums Withstood Every Mess We Threw at Them

We scattered crumbs, dust, and debris to determine which models could power through these piles of mess without a hiccup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

They’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

Below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

For models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

In each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

To better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

Our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

We are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As new components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

We’ll soon be testing the Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum, which is an uprgraded version of our previous Best Overall recommendation, the Qrevo S. The latest model offers much of the same functionality, along with a few improvements—and a couple trade-offs.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. The spinning mop heads reach 200 rotations per minute and lift 10 millimeters, helping prevent carpets and area rugs from getting wet as the robot vacuum moves between thresholds. However, unlike the Qrevo S, the mop heads rely on air drying rather than using a hot air drying system, which could mean longer downtime between cleaning sessions.

Beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor plans, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

To support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

If you–or your pet–tend to shed a lot of hair, the Eureka J15 Pro robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. The base has a built-in, automatic hair cutting tool that slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have manually remove hair from the roller.

This robot vacuum isn’t lacking in power, either. It delivers 16,000 Pa suction for a deeper clean, and it works on a variety of floor types like carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile. The J15 Pro has advanced obstacle detection, and our tester, who has been using this model for months, tells us that it’s great at avoiding furniture, cords, pet toys, and over-friendly pets. It even takes a picture whenever it runs into something in its cleaning path, and you’re able to view the photo within the map afterwards in case it’s something that should be moved liked shoes and cords (or an animal).

The mopping feature is also effective at keeping your house clean. There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper clean, and they extend to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards. Our tester found the J15 Pro to be quiet on all modes, but Turbo is noticeably louder than the nighttime mode. You have control over suction power, though, so it doesn’t have to be running at full capacity constantly if you want to cut down on background noise.

She does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. There are a plethora of settings and options available, and while it’s easy to set up basic settings initially, it gets a lot more involved. Those who are really just looking for daily maintenance and don’t want all the bells and whistles may find this cumbersome.

As a first-time robot vacuum owner, our tester has been very pleased with his ongoing experience using the dreame X40 Ultra. It’s been able to take on dirt, dust, crumbs, and anything that his dog tracks inside, and exceeded expectations on hardwood floors. There are a few places it struggled to reach, like under a coffee table and TV stand, but we chalk that up to a height issue rather than capability concerns.

The X40 Ultra has 12,000 Pa of suction power, and a liftable, extendable side brush that gets close to wall corners and furniture legs. To protect rugs and carpets from getting wet, the robot vacuum either detaches the mop heads or lifts them to 10.5 millimeters, preventing any wet and dry mess combinations.

The app also allows you to program no-go zones, including rugs or other problem areas like staircases. Even with pet toys laying around the house, the X40 was able to navigate and map the layout with ease, all while avoiding these obstacles.

The mopping feature is a favorite for our tester. If you’re constantly on the go, having a robot vacuum capable of mopping on a daily basis is a real game changer. And thanks to auto-empty and auto-refill tanks, it’s really a set-it-and-forget-it device. We only suggest that you run the robot vacuum overnight so you aren’t disturbed by its run cycle. (Waking up to beautiful, clean floors is fun, too.)

Full Dreame X40 Ultra Robotic Vacuum Review

Ecovacs has been around since the late 90’s, and the brand introduced its first Deebot in 2007. Needless to say, its designs have come along way, and one of the latest versions piqued our interest for one main reason: stain removal.

Most often, robot vacuums with mopping capability can only handle fresh spills on hardwood and tile, not the stubborn, dried-on stuff. The Deebot X12 is trying to change that. It uses an AI camera and infrared stain detector to identify spills, splatters, and even muddy paw prints. Then, it deploys two jets with cleaning solution at up to 46,000 Pascals to loosen residue for the mop roller head to pick up. This could potentially save you from having to make a more detailed pass by hand.

The vacuum has capable power on carpet, too. It uses 22,000 Pascals of suction power to get rid or dirt, hair, and debris, and features an anti-tangle side and main brush to prevent hair from getting trapped around the bristles and roller.

The docking station is one of the more advanced designs we’ve seen in a robot vacuum. It has a bagless dustbin, power washing for the mop roller, and hot air drying. We’re looking forward to testing out this model and updating this guide accordingly with our findings.

Full Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicycle Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

The Qrevo CurvX is a newer design from Roborock, and we like that is has a slimmer build to fit under a wider variety of furniture, but still packs 22,000 Pa of suction power (the highest on our list). It’s equipped with a range of smart features, including pet recognition technology and two-way video calling (in the Roborock app) to interact with furry friends while you’re away, making it a great choice for households with animals.

The initial mapping process took a bit of time, but alas, this is a crucial step for an accurate layout of your home. Once the mapping was complete, the CurvX navigated efficiently, avoiding unnecessary paths and cleaning strategically as it went. During operation, the vacuum ran very quietly, especially when compared to other Roborock models we’ve experienced.

One of the biggest conveniences is the automatic dustbin emptying system, as it significantly reduces the need for manual maintenance. The tanks hold debris for up to seven weeks, and the water tank automatically refills the reservoir on the robot vacuum so you don’t have to.

The mop lifting and carpet detection performed well in our lab tests. When used in the concrete floor pen with obstacles like a small rug, it raised the heads with ease when transitioning between floor types. This ensured that carpets didn’t get wet during mopping sessions and the robot maintained the right cleaning mode. The edge mopping system is also a fantastic feature. The mop heads sit on arms that extend outwards for better reach, and they were able to get under and around table legs more efficiently.

That being said, this model isn’t without its limitations. In some of our mess tests, it missed detritus that was close to the pen walls, or “room edges,” despite the side brush kicking up the debris. It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Full Roborock Qrevo CruvX Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

If you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

The vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

One of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

Many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:

Eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

Roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

This navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

With this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM)

This triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each new model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for big homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

The most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

Throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

When set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

For homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

#6441. Intensive breathing exercises can create psychedelic ‘tripping’ effects by changing how the brain talks to itself

Intensive breathwork cut brain blood flow by about 45 percent in MRI scans, yet the depth of the altered state tracked brain networks, not the drop.

People who practice intensive breathwork (fast, nonstop breathing) for an hour describe something close to a psychedelic trip. They recount vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity with the universe, and no drug involved.

Inside an MRI scanner, the brain lost nearly half its usual blood supply during that experience. Yet how far the blood flow fell had nothing to do with how deep the experience went.

Christian Schmitz led the work at the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim, Germany. His colleagues came from the Medical Faculty Mannheim of Heidelberg University and the MIND Foundation in Berlin.

His team scanned the brains of 30 experienced breathwork practitioners during a single session, with no comparison group, so the findings are preliminary.

“Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood,” Schmitz said.

“Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate.”

Breathing hard and fast for a long time removes carbon dioxide from the blood faster than the body makes it.

Carbon dioxide is one of the main signals that keeps the brain’s small blood vessels open. When it drops, those vessels tighten and less blood gets through.

The team measured blood flow through the brain’s grey matter at the moment each person rated the experience strongest.

At this point, blood flow had fallen from about 30 to about 16 milliliters per 100 grams of tissue per minute. That is a drop of about 45 percent, which is a large change for something a person does on purpose.

Earlier studies have reported signs of the brain not getting enough oxygen when flow falls by 50 to 60 percent. The average here came close to that limit and stayed below it.

A 2025 study of the same kind of intensive breathwork measured a drop of 41.6 percent, and Schmitz’s team wrote that the two results agree.

The 30 volunteers were between 26 and 64 years old, and half were women. Most had practiced intensive breathwork for one to three years, typically less than once a month.

Anyone with a history of a psychiatric or neurological disorder was left out, and so was anyone who had taken a psychedelic in the previous three months.

Each person lay in the scanner and breathed in a continuous circle, with no pause between breaths, for as long as they chose. That ran from about 36 to 96 minutes. Music played the whole time, either their own or the study’s.

Every 12 minutes, the room light came on and the person pressed one of four buttons to rate the experience against the strongest breathwork session of their life.

Medical staff supervised every session, and monitoring continued for at least an hour afterward.

The experiences were strong: on the four-point scale, the average rating at the peak was 3.5, and the most common answer was the top mark.

Within an hour of the session’s end, each person filled in a standard questionnaire on altered states. The profile that came back was dominated by a sense of boundlessness and a drop in alertness, with milder visual changes.

Psychedelics produce a closely similar profile, the authors wrote. The scores were lower, though, than people typically report after a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin.

A person whose blood flow fell the most was no more likely to report an intense experience than a person whose flow fell the least. The size of the drop predicted neither the button ratings during the session nor the questionnaire scores afterward.

One reading, the authors wrote, is that the drop works like a threshold. Once blood flow falls far enough, altered states become possible, and falling further doesn’t deepen them.

The team also looked at the default mode network, a set of brain regions that are active together when a person is resting and thinking about themselves.

Psilocybin and LSD reliably weaken the coordination inside that network, and the team expected intensive breathwork to do the same.

Resting scans before and after the session showed no overall change in how tightly those regions worked together. But the people whose network connections weakened the most reported the most intense altered states.

The team found that link under one way of cleaning the scan data and not under another, so they called it tentative. The drop in blood flow didn’t predict the network change either.

So the authors described two partly separate things: a brain getting far less blood and, in some people, a reorganizing network that goes with the experience itself.

The team presented the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich in October.

Everyone in the study was an experienced practitioner, so how a first-timer’s brain responds is an open question.

The network scans were taken after the breathing stopped, not during it, because the chest and head movement of circular breathing ruins that kind of scan. Any change that faded quickly was missed.

The team didn’t measure carbon dioxide in the breath, and there was no comparison session of plain rest. Music played throughout, which the authors wrote can change the same network on its own.

Hana Adolphi at the Central Institute of Mental Health co-coordinated the study and is a co-author on the publication. “Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness,” she said.

“Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance,” she added.

Whether the network change happens during the breathing itself, rather than after it, is the question this design couldn’t answer.

The authors wrote that future studies need scanning methods that can cope with the motion of hard breathing, and a plain resting session to compare against.

The full study was published in the journal Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry.

#6440. A farmer in Mexico saw the ground split open in his cornfield, then watched a volcano grow to 1,391 feet tall

In 1943, Mexico's Parícutin volcano erupted from a farmer's cornfield, growing rapidly and burying two villages during nine years of activity.

On February 20, 1943, farmer Dionisio Pulido watched a fissure open in his field near the village of Parícutin, in the Mexican state of Michoacán. Smoke rose from the crack, along with a hissing sound and a smell of sulfur.

Within a week, the new cone stood more than 490 feet (150 meters) tall. When the eruption ended in 1952, it had risen 1,391 feet (424 meters) above the cornfield where it began.

Lava buried two villages along the way. Parícutin was the first volcano whose eruption modern scientists observed in detail from its birth, according to the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS).

Starting around February 5 to 7, 1943, local witnesses felt about two weeks of earthquake activity before the eruption.

Felipe Cuara Amezcua, then municipal president of San Juan Parangaricutiro, later reported that the tremors grew until more than 200 shook the area in a single day.

On February 20, Pulido went to his farm to prepare the fields for the spring sowing. He had owned the land for 31 years.

Smithsonian mineralogist William F. Foshag and Mexican geologist Jenaro González R. later collected his account and his wife’s. A 1956 U.S. Geological Survey bulletin printed them in English translation.

At about 4 p.m., Pulido left his wife, Paula, and went to burn a pile of branches. She had been hearing underground noise and thunder.

“About 4 p. m., after talking to my husband, I heard a kind of loud whistle,” Paula Pulido recalled.

“I saw that it was a kind of fissure that had only a depth of half a meter,” Pulido said.

He then saw the ground swell by about 6.6 to 8 feet (2 to 2.5 meters), while gray smoke or dust rose from the crack.

“Immediately more smoke began to rise, with a hiss or whistle, loud and continuous,” he recounted.

Frightened, he mounted his mare and galloped to the village where his family was waiting.

Accounts from Pulido and other witnesses gave “the first adequate account of the birth of a new volcano,” Foshag and González wrote.

One of the first photographs of the eruption, taken at 6 p.m. on February 20, shows an ash plume rising from the new vent. By midnight, the cone was about 20 feet (6 meters) high.

On the morning of February 21, a strong earthquake caused panic. People from Parícutin fled to San Juan Parangaricutiro, and many from San Juan went on to Angahuan or Uruapan.

A photograph from February 21 shows the cone about 100 feet (30 meters) tall, just rising above the treetops. After six days of activity, it reached 548 feet (167 meters).

The first lava flow, called the Quitzocho flow, moved north over cornfields prepared for planting. Mexican geologist Ezequiel Ordóñez estimated that the early lava advanced about 10 feet (3 meters) an hour.

Ash fell too. It piled up deeper than 6 inches (15 centimeters) over an area of 116 square miles (300 square kilometers) around the volcano.

When the first phase of activity ended on October 19, 1943, the original vent had built a cone about 1,200 feet (365 meters) high.

Pulido’s home village lay only 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) northwest of the new cone. Its 733 residents had to abandon it for good four months after the eruption began, and lava later flowed over the site.

Starting in January 1944, a new phase sent out the Taquí lava flows, which spread over about 7 square miles (18 square kilometers) by 1945.

In July 1944, lava surrounded the church of San Juan Parangaricutiro. Its tower still stands in the middle of a lava flow, the IUGS notes.

In all, the volcano’s lavas reached up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) from the vent and formed a field of about 9.7 square miles (25 square kilometers).

The Mexican government gave displaced residents new land in Caltzontzín, 17 miles (27 kilometers) to the southeast.

Parícutin was “the first well-documented example of an eruption of a monogenetic volcanic cone in historical time,” according to a 1993 USGS film report.

A monogenetic cone forms during a single eruptive episode. Parícutin, active for about nine years, gave scientists an unprecedented chance to follow such a volcano through its full life cycle.

An international group documented the activity in real time. Celedonio Gutiérrez, a resident of San Juan who kept a diary from the first day, worked with U.S. scientists throughout the eruption.

In 1990, volcanologists I. Yokoyama and S. de la Cruz-Reyna analyzed the precursory earthquakes of the 1943 eruption, a type of signal that comes before eruptions.

In 1985, decades after the eruption stopped, a fumarole at Parícutin still measured 883°F (473°C). The cone is one of more than 1,400 vents in the Michoacán-Guanajuato volcanic field.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program.

#6439. Worker or queen? A genetic advantage may shape a fire ant’s future

A study of fire ants suggests a “selfish” supergene influences body size, potentially giving some ants a better chance of becoming queens.

Most red imported fire ants become workers. A few become queens, the largest ants in the colony and the ones that lay eggs.

How large an ant grows during development helps determine whether it becomes a worker or a queen.

A new study suggests that genes also influence this process.

In colonies with several queens, ants carrying a particular version of a large group of genes were more common among the biggest workers and future queens.

Haolin “Horace” Zeng and Brendan Hunt, insect researchers at the University of Georgia, studied this pattern in lab colonies.

Their work offers a clue to why these genes keep spreading, even though they can have drawbacks for the ants carrying them.

Some fire ant colonies have just one queen laying eggs, while others have many. A group of more than 500 genes helps determine which kind of colony develops.

These genes sit close together on a chromosome, a structure that carries DNA. They pass from parent to offspring together as a package called a supergene.

“We call them supergenes because the genes are tightly linked and inherited together, almost like one big gene,” explained Hunt, an associate professor in UGA’s entomology department.

The package comes in two versions. Scientists call the older version B and the newer one b, which appeared about one million years ago.

Ants in single-queen colonies have two copies of B, written as BB.

In invasive populations with several queens per colony, every egg-laying queen has one copy of each version, written as Bb.

Queens with the Bb combination weigh less and have more trouble starting colonies alone than BB queens. Yet the b version continues to spread.

Scientists describe it as a “selfish genetic element” because it improves its own chances of reaching the next generation, even when it does not help the ant carrying it.

Becoming a queen gives a female ant the opportunity to pass her genes to the next generation.

“If you want to pass down a gene, you’d better become a queen. You don’t want to become a worker,” Zeng said.

Young ants grow as larvae before becoming pupae, the stage when they change into adults. A natural chemical called juvenile hormone can delay the move out of the larval stage, giving them more time to eat and grow.

The researchers wanted to find out whether ants with the b version responded differently to this hormone.

In spring 2024, they collected colonies with one queen and colonies with several queens from Clarke and Oconee counties in Georgia.

They used these ants to set up small lab colonies without queens.

Each held about 2,500 workers, and all colonies received the same total weight of young ants at different developmental stages.

Some colonies received one meal containing methoprene, an artificial chemical that acts like juvenile hormone and is also used as an insecticide.

The others received a meal without it, and workers passed the food to the larvae.

Between 15 and 24 days after that meal, the team collected and weighed worker pupae. The middle weight, or median, was about three times higher in treated colonies than in untreated colonies.

The researchers then checked the genes of 1,049 worker pupae and 195 queen pupae from colonies with several queens. They compared the ants’ genes with their weight.

Ants carrying the b version became more common as body weight increased.

Here, ‘carrying the supergene’ refers specifically to the b version.

“Among the smallest workers, about half carried the supergene,” Hunt said. “That proportion increased to roughly 65% among the largest workers and 75% to 83% among queens.”

On average, BB pupae weighed about 19% less than Bb pupae. But the heaviest ants in each group weighed about the same, so the b version did not raise the upper limit on size.

Instead, ants carrying b reached the larger sizes more often.

The hormone treatment increased size by about the same amount in both groups, suggesting that a major difference in their response to this hormone did not explain the pattern.

The share of Bb ants also rose with weight at a similar rate among workers and queens.

That suggests the gene package affects body size, which then helps shape whether an ant becomes a queen, rather than having a separate effect on queen development.

“To me, it highlights that, through a developmental mechanism involving body size, a genetic element can alter caste outcomes and basically cheat its way into making a queen,” Hunt said.

The team next looked for genes that might explain the size difference. Scientists do not yet have a full record of which genes become more active as fire ant larvae grow into workers or queens.

The researchers therefore used existing data from pharaoh ants, which belong to the same ant subfamily.

Earlier work on adult fire ants had identified 191 genes that were more active in Bb ants than in BB ants.

Of those, 34 were also more active in pharaoh ant larvae developing into queens. That overlap was larger than the researchers would expect by chance.

One gene, called gas8, appeared in every comparison and sits within the fire ant supergene.

DNA near the start of gas8 is also more loosely packed in Bb fire ants, which fits with the gene being more active.

The team still does not know how the gene package changes growth.

Perhaps large BB larvae die more often before becoming pupae, or perhaps some Bb larvae spend longer eating and growing before moving to the next stage.

A computer simulation showed that extra growing time could produce the pattern seen in the study. Giving Bb larvae a better chance of continuing to a larger size could also explain it.

Workers might treat larvae carrying b more favorably, but that alone seems unlikely to explain the findings.

An earlier experiment found extra Bb queen pupae even when only BB workers raised them.

Researchers have not yet tested what gas8 does as ants develop. Experiments with fire ant larvae will be needed to find out.

Comparisons with other animals that carry supergenes could answer a wider question: do these gene packages often spread by changing how animals grow, or how long they spend growing?

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6438. Neanderthal heel bones reveal feet built for a demanding life

Neanderthals may have had flatter feet that helped them handle heavy loads and stay steady on rough ground.

A flatter foot may have helped Neanderthals support their heavy bodies and stay steady on rough ground.

A new study of fossil heel bones suggests that Neanderthal feet usually rolled inward and had a lower arch along the outside edge.

Researchers think this build may have suited the demands of their daily lives.

The study also found differences within our own species, Homo sapiens.

People who lived in Bologna, Italy, in the 19th and 20th centuries had slimmer heel bones than prehistoric hunter-gatherers, and their footwear and less active lives may help explain why.

Rita Sorrentino, now a professor at the University of Palermo, led the study, which University of Bologna professor Maria Giovanna Belcastro coordinated.

Belcastro said the analysis allowed the team “to highlight both an extraordinary biomechanical adaptation to withstand heavy loads and rough terrains, and the impact of modern life and footwear on our feet.”

No one can watch a Neanderthal walk, so the researchers looked for clues in the bones left behind. They used laser scans and CT scans to create 3D models of 71 adult heel bones.

Seven belonged to Neanderthals from sites in France, Spain, and Belgium. The youngest came from Spy Cave in Belgium and belonged to one of the last known Neanderthals in Europe.

The other 64 belonged to Homo sapiens. The oldest came from hunter-gatherers at Qafzeh and Skhul caves in Israel and dated to between 120,000 and 90,000 years ago.

The sample also included later Ice Age hunter-gatherers, Iron Age farmers from Sicily, and 46 people from a Bologna cemetery collection.

The researchers considered the Bologna group the least physically active population in the study.

The researchers marked 276 points along the edges and curved surfaces of each digital bone.

These points let them compare the heels in detail, while software estimated missing points on broken fossils from the parts that remained.

Neanderthal heels stood out in every comparison with Homo sapiens.

They were shorter from front to back, wider from side to side, and taller, although their overall size fell within the range seen in our species.

The biggest difference appeared at the back of the heel, where the Achilles tendon attaches. From behind, this area looked oval in Neanderthals and more triangular in Homo sapiens.

Neanderthals also had a much smaller bump underneath the heel, where a ligament that supports the arch attaches.

The researchers suggest this ligament may have provided less support, allowing the foot to bend more easily.

Belcastro linked the sturdy heels to the rest of the Neanderthal body.

“The robustness of the heel reflects the overall body structure of Neanderthals, which is characterized by a remarkable muscular and bone mass and an extremely intense level of physical activity,” Belcastro said.

“These physical characteristics indicate an adaptation aimed at promoting a greater load-bearing capacity on the back of the foot and a high mobility on uneven ground.”

The joints offered another clue. Where the heel meets the ankle bone, the joint surfaces were flatter and wider toward the outside of the foot.

That shape suggests Neanderthal feet normally rolled inward, a movement specialists call pronation.

Earlier research by Sorrentino’s group found signs of the same posture in Neanderthal ankle bones, on the other side of this joint.

In living people, rolling the foot inward brings more of those joint surfaces into contact and helps spread the load.

Neanderthals are thought to have carried more body mass than Homo sapiens, including more muscle, so this posture may have helped support their weight.

The researchers also propose that Neanderthals had a lower outer arch and a more flexible middle section of the foot.

Together, those features may have helped them stay steady as they crossed uneven ground.

An earlier study by the team found that a Neanderthal midfoot bone shared some features with those of adults diagnosed with flexible flatfoot. Most of those adults were overweight or obese.

Extra body weight may make feet roll inward and flatten their arches in people today. Still, similarities in bone shape do not prove that Neanderthal feet worked in exactly the same way.

Some differences may reflect ancestry rather than daily habits.

A small tunnel between the heel and ankle bones was shortest in Neanderthals, and its short length in other ancient human fossils suggests an inherited trait.

Within Homo sapiens, however, heel shape tended to vary with lifestyle.

In some ways, hunter-gatherers and even Iron Age farmers who also foraged had heels more like those of Neanderthals than those of the Bologna group.

Fossil footprints suggest that Neanderthals in Europe and later Ice Age Homo sapiens walked barefoot.

The Bologna group habitually wore heavy shoes and boots at work, and their heels differed from those of every earlier Homo sapiens group in the study.

Rigid footwear limits how far a foot can tilt from side to side.

The researchers suggest this restriction helped shape the joint at the front of the Bologna heels, which was taller and more curved.

The team also linked the Bologna group’s slimmer heels to footwear and a less active city life. But shoes alone cannot explain every difference.

“The morphology of our skeleton is not only the product of a strict genetic program, but also the consequence of physical stimuli and our daily life habits,” Belcastro said.

Ancestry, nutrition, and environment can also affect heel shape, the researchers wrote. The comparisons suggest that daily life matters, but they do not show how much each influence contributed.

The Neanderthal findings rest on just seven heels, several of which were damaged at the back and needed partial reconstruction.

The researchers also grouped men and women together because the samples did not allow them to test whether sex affected the results.

All the bones came from adults, leaving another question unanswered: how did Neanderthal heels develop that shape?

Their feet may have grown differently, responded to the strain of walking during childhood, or both.

A lower Neanderthal arch remains a hypothesis because bones alone cannot show exactly how a foot moved.

The researchers want future work to combine these shape comparisons with 3D models of foot motion to test the idea.

The study is published in the Journal of Human Evolution.
