Scientists in the U.S. and Canada are decoding grizzly bears' behavior to learn how they navigate a human-dominated world. What they find could build a safer future for both species.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Across 53 challenging days between fall 2020 and spring 2021, a 360-pound (160 kilograms) young male grizzly bear nicknamed "Lingenpolter" tried to cross Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times. High-resolution GPS tracking showed him moving parallel to four lanes of roaring traffic, bouncing off the highway like a furry pinball as he searched for a gap.

Eventually, Lingenpolter beat the odds, probably by slipping under a river bridge. But his hero's journey shows what a formidable barrier a busy highway can be for wildlife, Cecily Costello, a research wildlife biologist at Montana's Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks, told Live Science. "It is easy to imagine the difficulty this grizzly bear experienced trying to reach the other side," Costello said.

A map of all the places Lingenpolter attempted to cross the road before making it across.

This past May, another grizzly wasn't so lucky. Braving a crossing near one of Lingenpolter's attempts, the 27-year-old male bear was struck and killed by a truck, triggering a multicar rollover.

It's crucial for grizzly bears (Ursus arctos), also known as brown bears, to have room to roam. When they can't move between populations to mate, small groups get genetically isolated. And what's true for bears can also be true for other wildlife. "It's really challenging to be a small, fragmented population," said Michael Proctor, a wildlife biologist at Birchdale Ecological Ltd., a Canada-based environmental consulting firm. Such fragmentation is "one of the mechanisms by which we lose entire communities, and sometimes whole species," he told Live Science.

Nowhere is this challenge more urgent than in the 2,100 mile long (3,400 kilometers) region stretching along the spine of the Rocky Mountains between Yellowstone in Wyoming and the Yukon in northern Canada. The area, which spans five U.S. states, two Canadian provinces, and more than 75 Indigenous territories "represents the most intact, connected, wild, large mountain region in the world," Jordan Reeves, program director of landscape connectivity at the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y), which aims to secure connectivity throughout the region told Live Science.

The terrain between Yellowstone and the Yukon is the most intact wild large mountain region, and is crucial for bear migration.

But as highways, rail lines, and human development fragment its valleys, maintaining connected pathways for grizzly bears across this landscape has become a challenge.

Grizzlies range across vast, diverse terrain, spanning high-elevation alpine habitats, mid-mountain slopes, and low valley bottoms, which means safeguarding their movement can also protect passageways for coexisting species, including wolverines, mountain goats, elk and bighorn sheep, Proctor said. That's why researchers are trying to understand why, where and when grizzlies move. And what stops them in their tracks.

"We're looking at how a bear sees the world," Andrew Derocher, a bear biologist at the University of Alberta who has used GPS collars on grizzly bears to trace their movements, told Live Science.

When Sarah Sells started her graduate studies in animal behavior, her supervisor told her to "try to crawl into their fur brains and understand how they think," Sells told Live Science. Although we can't recreate exactly what's going on between a grizzly's ears, GPS collars that track animal movement hourly can tell scientists a lot about how animals behave, said Sells, who is currently the assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey's Montana Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit.

That tracking data is starting to produce an incredibly detailed picture not just of where bears go but also how and why they're making those choices.

"Bears are food finding machines," Chris Servheen, a bear biologist with the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Bear Specialist Group, told Live Science. "So remembering where they found food is critical to their success in life."

Using a combination of telemetry data (information collected by tracking devices) and movement modeling, Derocher and colleagues have investigated how well grizzlies remember where food is and when it is best to visit a foraging patch. Derocher's research showed that about two-thirds of the bears have a great memory for where and in what season they previously found food. His tracking data also revealed that wild bears generally avoid humans. But bears have only a few months to fatten up for winter. If food is scarce, many bears go into human environments and sometimes get killed, Proctor said.

The data is also offering insight into different bear "personalities." Bears are ultimately individuals, with their own traits and quirks, Servheen said.

A young male bear named Lingenpolter tried to cross the Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times before successfully making it across.

Tracking data suggests that a lot of bear behavior is transmitted culturally via a mother's influence. Sometimes, the wrong behavior can get passed down to the next generation, Servheen said. For example, an infamous female grizzly known as 399 jaywalked potentially hundreds of times in the Jackson Hole valley in Wyoming while managing to keep her distance from humans. Her 20-odd cubs learned to follow her example, but they lacked her strategic caution. Several were killed by vehicles or management euthanizations.

"It's a risky thing to teach your kids to do stuff like that," Servheen said. "And her offspring weren't as smart as she was."

Further north along the region between Yellowstone and the Yukon, Proctor's first DNA survey across 1,500 square miles (4,000 square kilometers) of southern British Columbia in the late 1990s shattered his illusion that the bears, along with bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) and other species in this province, were free to roam. Instead, he found a "cracked windshield" landscape, where roads and human sprawl had fractured the wilderness into isolated genetic islands. In the 2000s, the genetic diversity of the South Selkirk grizzly bears — a detatched subpopulation inhabiting southeastern British Columbia, northern Idaho, and northeastern Washington — was so low, for example, that biologists feared the bears wouldn't survive.

But Proctor and his colleagues went on to use bear movement data to model pathways through human-settled valleys. Proctor was so convinced about the viability of one potential corridor that he paid 10,000 Canadian dollars ($7,000) of his own money to buy a key piece of land right in the middle of it. "That was the first canoe over the waterfall of purchasing connectivity land," Proctor said

Proctor’s land secured a segment of a crucial connectivity corridor and, in the following years, he and other scientists partnered with trusts to purchase other land parcels, build fences, and establish safe corridors for grizzlies in the Creston Valley in southeastern British Columbia. These actions helped bears move north and south (sometimes across the border) and between the South Selkirk Mountains and Purcell Mountains. The researchers then watched bears like "Captain Hook," who'd been shot in the leg, hobble into the South Selkirks and breed with eight females. By 2021, nine immigrant bears had produced 27 new offspring within the population.

"This is gene flow; this is connectivity," Proctor said. "We took a completely isolated population and pretty much recovered it."

The peaks of the Purcell and Rocky Mountain ranges frame the Rocky Mountain Trench insoutheastern British Columbia—a core component of the Yellowstone to Yukon region. Steeptopography forces both wildlife and human activity into the same low-elevation valley bottoms.

Despite efforts to safeguard corridors through human occupied landscape, roads continue to stop bears in their tracks. When Servheen tracked bears near Highway 2 in northwest Montana, he found that many of the grizzlies avoided the highway altogether and those that crossed did so at night. But he also found that the bears' crossings clustered in specific sections of the road. Finding the crossing zones has helped researchers identify good locations for constructing overpasses and underpasses on many busy highways, but a crossing structure on its own is not enough, Servheen cautioned.

A bear's memory for where to find food is exemplary, but there's no special reward in a bear's brain for crossing a road safely — only a fatal penalty when they don't, Servheen said. So conservationists can't rely on bears to remember where crossings are. Instead, they must build fencing along the highway to funnel wildlife into the underpasses or overpasses. Then, the immediate land on each side needs to allow animals safe passage. "Otherwise, you have a bridge to nowhere," Servheen said.

Now researchers such as Sells are trying to use data about bears' likeliest routes to determine potential corridors in locations where they have little tracking data or where few bears live yet.

To do this, Sells is developing a virtual "Sims for Bears" that recreates the Continental Divide Ecosystem in Montana. In the life-simulation video game "The Sims," players give virtual humans personality traits, preferences and needs, and then drop them into a virtual environment to see how they behave.

Sells built the model using the GPS collaring data from 65 grizzly bears navigating individual paths through greenery, riparian areas and around forests and roads. Then, she "parachutes" an individual digital bear into a detailed computer simulation of real-world terrain and has them take thousands of virtual steps. By running these multiple simulated bears through thousands of iterations across the digital terrain, the researchers can watch where the virtual bears repeatedly choose to walk, effectively creating a map of predicted movement corridors.

Sells has used the model to predict how grizzly bears might recolonize the Bitterroot ecosystem of Idaho and Montana, which Lingenpolter was heading toward when attempting to cross Interstate 90.

To get to the Bitterroot Mountains, bears must pass through a valley filled with people, roads, garbage and fruit trees. "So knowing where they are more likely to end up is helpful to address things that could be difficult for humans or bears," Sells told Live Science.

The data is also confirming that the greatest barrier bears face comes from human contact or transportation infrastructure across the entire Yellowstone-to-Yukon region. Studies from across west-central North America report that humans directly or indirectly caused between 77% and 90% of grizzly bear deaths from 1989 to 2015. Hunting, managed kills in urban areas and road and rail collisions all take a toll.

Bears running across the road in Glacier National Park.

Bears in the wild usually avoid people, but some bears seek out human-dominated areas because they know these places are a source of food. People move to the Elk Valley in southeastern British Columbia because they love nature, but then they plant apple trees in their backyard, which attract bears, said Clayton Lamb, a wildlife scientist at the nonprofit Biodiversity Pathways.

Quickly, a bear eating backyard apples gets labeled a "problem bear," "when really it is a 'people problem,'" Lamb told Live Science.

Even human recreation takes a toll on bears' health and ability to move freely. Lamb's research has shown that grizzly bears try to avoid areas next to busy cycling and hiking trails.

To minimize human-bear conflict, Michelle McLellan, a wildlife ecologist at Biodiversity Pathways, has tracked trail use by both people and grizzlies in the West Kootenay region of British Columbia. McLellan documented people's habits using trail cameras and apps such as Strava Metro. Her research shows that the bears use the trails to move quickly between foraging spots but have learned not to use the trails that are most popular with humans. Consequently, the Nelson Cycling Club decided to close certain trails in the spring and cautioned riders about when and how to use the open trails. "Ride aware, make noise, slow down when needed," the club cautioned in its May newsletter.

Working with information from McLellan, the club has cut back overgrown vegetation along sight lines to prevent mountain bikers from startling bears at close range. They've also constructed wooden platforms on sections of trails that clatter and rumble as bikes pass over them, giving bears early notice of approaching riders. "The key is to not surprise them by making a lot of noise." McLellan told Live Science, noting that grizzlies are more likely to attack if they are surprised.

One advantage of having human mountain biking and hiking trails concentrated close to towns is that it focuses recreation into specific areas, Lamb said. Keeping trails condensed supplies multiple accessible paths and reduces humans encroaching on true wilderness — prime bear habitat. "The goal would be to ensure that there's sufficient recreation opportunities for people to stay healthy and connected to their local landscape while ensuring that wildlife can still move around and access their habitats," Lamb said

As humans increasingly live, work and play in bear territory, it's important to recognize the impact on the animals, Servheen said. "The bears never get a day off," he said. "Every day, they're trying to stay away from people and make a living in a place with multiple people on the landscape."

Bears expend a lot of much-needed energy trying to avoid people, and they won't be able to do that forever, Servheen said. As humans increase the development of private lands and recreation in bear territory, the squeeze is on. "There's going to be more conflicts with bears, and more dead bears," Servheen said.

The bears have done their part, Lamb said. His research has shown that bears living near humans are adapting by becoming mostly nocturnal, which reduces their odds of clashing with humans. "So, we need to meet them where they are at and see what we can do to share the space," Lamb said.

On the human side, people need to make it less tempting for bears to be in human dominated areas, McLellan said. That means keeping garbage stowed and making sure there is no ripe fruit available. "If you live rurally, you want them to be able to pass through your property but not linger near your home or in your front yard," McLellan said.

Bears have proved to be adaptable and persistent; Lingenpolter tried to cross the highway dozens of times before finding a way under. However, Servheen warned that we are putting them in a tough spot. To keep bear populations stable, scientists need data on bear behavior to help inform land management policies that create safe pathways for grizzlies to move through human dominated areas and regulate recreation with bears in mind, Servheen said.

"If we want to have bears in the future, we need to think about the needs bears have for some level of space on the landscape," Servheen said.

Securing that space across the vast Yellowstone to Yukon landscape requires more than just land acquisitions and highway overpasses — it requires increasing public awareness and counteracting the perception that bears are inherently aggressive and irrational, Proctor said. If people understand bear behavior, they can learn to act in ways that neither attract bears nor threaten them. And understanding the totality of bears’ strong drive to survive, and protect each other, can elicit empathy and motivation to protect this iconic species.

Early in his career, Proctor captured, immobilized and radio-collared a mother grizzly with her two yearlings, or newly adolescent bears. While the research team worked, the young bears circled quietly at a distance. When the scientists finally stepped back and the mother began to stir, the yearlings approached cautiously. As the mother's groggy head rested on a log, the yearlings' long-clawed front paws delicately explored the radio collar. Then, each one rested its head directly on hers, to form a quiet pile of three bear heads.

"They just wanted to touch mom after this ordeal," Proctor said. "Yes, grizzlies can be rough and dangerous but they can also be gentle at times," Proctor said.

Reporting and travel for this story was supported by the Sitka Foundation and the Science Media Centre of Canada.

#6435. Methane emissions stayed stubbornly high despite a federal push to cut them

Satellite data show U.S. oil and gas methane emissions stayed nearly flat from 2019 to 2024, even as production grew and federal policies shifted.

Congress created the first federal methane fee in 2022 to encourage oil and gas companies to reduce emissions.

Satellite measurements now show that methane emissions from the sector remained near 11 million tons (10 million metric tons) a year from 2019 to 2024, with a slight increase in the final year.

The findings reveal no detectable decline following the law’s passage, though much of its enforcement framework had yet to take effect.

Methane emissions per unit of oil and gas produced fell by about 11% over the six years.

The researchers linked that decline mainly to new pipelines, better equipment, and earlier leak rules.

Ao Chen, a doctoral student at Johns Hopkins University, led the work with Scot Miller, an associate professor of environmental health and engineering there.

Colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin and McGill University took part.

Methane is nearly 30 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat, though it lasts a shorter time in the air. That makes it the second most important greenhouse gas to cut, Miller said.

Two instruments in orbit, Europe’s TROPOMI and Japan’s GOSAT, measure how much of it sits in the air below them.

The team fed roughly 2,000 of those readings a day over the lower 48 states into a model of how wind moves gas around. Then they ran it backward to work out where the methane came from.

The result is a map of emissions in boxes about 35 miles (55 kilometers) on a side, one for every day from 2019 to 2024.

Deciding how much of each box’s methane came from oil and gas rather than cattle or wetlands relies on existing inventories.

The team’s eight model runs show that choice can shift the oil and gas total by up to 20%.

The satellite totals ran about 17% above the EPA’s own inventory from 2019 to 2022. Earlier aerial and satellite studies have found the same gap, and some found it far wider.

Oil and gas methane across the lower 48 stayed between 10.3 million and 11.5 million tons (9.3 to 10.4 million metric tons) every year of the study.

It fell by about 640,000 tons (580,000 metric tons) from 2019 to 2023, then rose by about 230,000 tons (210,000 metric tons) in 2024.

Production, meanwhile, grew 8.5% over the same six years, so the methane released per barrel of oil and gas fell by 11.1%, or about 2.2% a year.

Most of that drop came between 2020 and 2022, before any new federal rule took hold.

“The good news is that emissions have not markedly increased, as many scientists feared would happen after an enormous increase in natural gas production in the decades following the hydraulic fracturing boom,” he said.

“The bad news is that oil and gas production is still a large percentage of U.S. methane emissions, and we do not find any evidence that a flurry of federal legislation had an impact on emissions.”

The Inflation Reduction Act created the Waste Emissions Charge, a fee on methane from large oil and gas facilities that was to begin in 2024.

It also set aside $1.36 billion to help companies find and fix leaks. The EPA finalized its own methane rules for new and existing wells in 2024.

Much of that framework had yet to take effect during the study.

The fee’s details stayed unsettled, and the rules for existing facilities gave states until 2026 to file their plans. Then Congress voided the fee rule in early 2025.

The EPA had projected the two measures together would cut 2024 emissions by about 420,000 tons (380,000 metric tons). The satellites saw an increase instead.

“We don’t see a detectable decrease in emissions after the Inflation Reduction Act,” Chen said.

“Of course, there’s no way to test the counterfactual. It’s possible that without the Inflation Reduction Act, methane emissions would be much higher.”

The biggest drop came from the biggest emitter.

Texas oil and gas methane fell 14%, from about 3.9 million tons (3.5 million metric tons) in 2019 to 3.3 million tons (3.0 million metric tons) in 2024. The state has no climate target.

The Gulf Coast Express line opened in late 2019, and the Whistler and Matterhorn Express lines followed, carrying gas from the Permian Basin to the coast and to Houston.

Pipeline access can allow producers to sell gas that might otherwise be flared or vented. Rising exports of liquefied natural gas made that gas worth more.

States with climate targets, among them California, Colorado, and New Mexico, cut oil and gas methane at rates that overlapped with states that have none.

Their inventories were more accurate, though. The satellite estimate was 3.6 times Texas’s official count and 5.8 times Oklahoma’s, while New Mexico’s matched.

California has pledged to cut its total methane 40% below 2013 levels by 2030.

That means cutting roughly 560,000 tons (510,000 metric tons) in four years, against about 130,000 tons (120,000 metric tons) over the past ten.

Colorado’s case is murkier. Its oil and gas methane swings by more than 30% from one year to the next, wider than the 26% cut its 2025 target demands.

That variability makes progress toward the target difficult to assess.

The study cannot establish what emissions would have been without the federal measures.

Continued satellite monitoring will help researchers track whether future policies and industry changes produce sustained reductions.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6434. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6433. Archaeologists unearthed a Pompeii cupboard containing 38 coins and a bag of childhood charms that were buried in the 79 AD eruption

A Pompeii cupboard buried in 79 AD held 38 bronze coins, 36 from Nero's reign, 24 childhood charms in a cloth bag and, nearby, two young wood mice.

In a back room of House IX 11, 7 on Via dell’Abbondanza, archaeologists found the imprint of a wooden Pompeii cupboard in the volcanic ash.

The Pompeii Archaeological Park says it was never reopened after Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD. Inside were 38 bronze coins in a basket, 24 small charms in a cloth bag, tweezers, a lamp and pots.

The park put out the news on October 29, 2026, with a 37-page report by director Gabriel Zuchtriegel and six colleagues. They do not know who lived there or what happened to them.

The front of the house was dug in 1912. Inscriptions around the door gave the name Cornelius Maximus. They can no longer be seen, and the report calls the name very doubtful.

The back rooms were reached only now, in the last phase of a project on the neighboring Insula dei Casti Amanti, the city block named for the House of the Chaste Lovers.

The goal was to make the slope safe along the alley between blocks 11 and 12, so old metal scaffolding could come down.

The top layer was modern fill with plastic and bits of metal. Under it the team found a toilet built into a wall niche in room D. Room C held a satyr-face roof tile and a bronze pot.

Room B, about 14 by 12.6 feet (4.3 by 3.85 meters), was probably a dining room. Its yellow walls show birds, panthers, a peacock and dolphins. Domenico Esposito, of the Freie Universität Berlin, put them down to the painters of Via di Castricio, a known workshop.

Building or repair work was going on in the house when the volcano erupted, the report says. Upper floors rarely survive at Pompeii, and researchers have used staircases that lead nowhere in the House of Thiasus to work out what stood above.

Two tunnels had been cut into these rooms after the eruption, at a date the report cannot fix. The second, about 3.6 feet (1.1 meters) wide, came from the west and ended at the east wall of room B.

It wrecked the fill in the middle of the room but left the ash along the sides. In that ash, the team found the shape of a big cupboard in the southeast corner.

It had two parts, each about 6.6 feet (2 meters) long. One was about 3 feet (0.9 meters) deep and the other 2.3 feet (0.7 meters). Two iron pieces fixed it to the floor.

The roof came down and broke the top of the cupboard. Then a pyroclastic flow, a fast current of hot ash and gas, came in from the northwest and filled it. More than half of its height survived.

The cupboard held five jugs, flasks, cooking pots, a glass plate, a bronze lamp and an incense burner. A thin cup had a pine-cone-scale pattern. There was also a glass ointment bottle, bronze tweezers and a slate palette for grinding makeup.

In the south part was a small wooden box with a bronze catch. It held eight lead weights, six with iron handles, and the authors say these may have been used for trade.

About 8 inches (0.2 meters) from the box lay a lump of 38 bronze coins. They had been kept in a little basket of woven plant fiber. Only part of its bottom, about 4.7 inches (0.12 meters), was left.

Two coins were old and worn, one from Ebusus, now Ibiza, and one a sestertius of Claudius struck in the name of Germanicus.

The other 36 were struck under Nero between 64 and 67 AD: 26 asses, seven dupondii and three sestertii, all Roman coin denominations. Twenty-one are from 65 AD.

The report calls it a small reserve, maybe for day-to-day spending. The team did not harden the basket with consolidant, so other tests could still be done. Archaeobotanist Chiara Comegna looked at it under a stereo microscope in the park’s lab.

About 2 feet (0.6 meters) from the east edge, along the inner south wall, the team found 24 tiny objects in faience, bone, glass paste and rock crystal. Each had a hole for a string.

There are the gods Bes and Mercury, hands, feet, pine cones or grapes, beads, a knucklebone and a winged shoe.

Romans called these crepundia, from a Latin word for rattling. Children wore them as protection, and adults could hear them moving about. Some earlier finds like these were taken for magic kit.

The bag sat on a middle shelf. A post about 6 inches (0.15 meters) thick fell on that shelf, the shelf tilted, and the bag slid to the back and tore. Under the microscope the cloth shows a regular weave at about 0.04 inches (1 millimeter).

Adults sometimes kept these necklaces all their lives, and at the Porta Nocera cemetery they were put in graves. The park notes that many Romans lived far from their parents and childhood homes.

Zuchtriegel said the find lets the team read “the different traces of a life” together: “personal habits, work, memories.”

In small bedroom B1 next door, seven post holes about 6.6 feet (2 meters) up the walls showed where a wooden loft had been. On it sat a North African olive oil amphora, six lids, three flasks, two pots and a big storage jar.

The bottom of the broken amphora was sieved and gave 117 tiny bones. Zooarchaeologist Younes Naime put them in the genus Apodemus, most likely the wood mouse. Naime counted two animals at the very least. Neither had finished growing.

Wood mice normally live in fields and gardens, the park says, but they slip into attics and food stores whenever they smell a meal. The house mouse is a different species, and it has followed people around since before farming began.

Back in 2023, the park described two mice and a young black rat found in the slave quarters of the Civita Giuliana villa. Rodent bones have also come out of the old sewers of Herculaneum.

Did the people of the house die in the eruption? Or did they run, and never make it back for their things? The report admits the evidence cannot settle it, and that is fair.

The press release mentioned Tacitus, who wrote that property left without heirs was put to use after the disaster. The report itself plays that down.

That link needs more study before anyone ties it to this house, and wall paintings alone say little about how rich a family was.

DNA tests on Pompeii’s victims have shown how wrong old guesses about sex and family can be. Other finds have pointed to the public role of women in the city.

“We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of whoever lived in the house,” Zuchtriegel said. Still to come: a textile specialist for the cloth samples, and more digging along the north and south walls of room B, which are only partly cleared.

The coins and the bag of charms were still inside the cupboard when the ash filled it in 79 AD.

The full study was published in the journal E-Journal degli Scavi di Pompei.

#6432. The 8 Best Hot Tubs That You Can Buy Online

We broke down the best options across sizes, styles, and price points, plus what actually matters before you commit.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

At some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea. It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

For our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this big purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

We chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

We pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

In a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

We like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

There are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss

If you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

Our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

We have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

With 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

We like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

We do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the issues folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

Even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many users say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

If aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

It’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

If you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up quickly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

The full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

While Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub says it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

The DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

There are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

“The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” says Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

He notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he says. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”

Plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

They’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

The trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

Most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

If you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

It’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a big difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Courter said that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he says. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”

When it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

While hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”

When it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” says Courter.

Other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” says Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

When it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

This is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

“As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” says Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being said, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” says Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”

#6431. Van Gogh’s Starry Night shows a real night sky, study suggests

For decades, art historians and astronomers have wondered whether the sky of Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night shows real stars or imagined ones. A new study argues the stars are real — and that Van Gogh likely saw them a month later than most scholars thought.

The study, published Oct. 22 in Scientific Reports, comes from a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of the South Korean telescope maker SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University’s School of Space Research in Yongin.

By combining astronomical data, historical primary sources, and statistical analysis, the team narrowed the celestial alignments shown in the painting’s sky to a handful of late-July mornings.

They further suggest Van Gogh likely painted the eastern sky as seen from his asylum room in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, around 3 a.m. on July 22, 1889. That morning, a waning crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades — the V-shaped star cluster in Taurus the Bull — were all gathered in the same small patch of sky.

RELATED: Exploring the solar system through space art

In May 1889, Van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, a former monastery outside Saint-Rémy. The previous December, after a falling-out with fellow painter Paul Gauguin, he had cut off his left ear, and more breakdowns followed. At the asylum he kept working, producing some 150 paintings, including famous works like Almond Blossom and The Starry Night.

On June 18, he wrote to his brother Theo that he had begun “a new study of a starry sky.” For most scholars, that line anchored the painting to the mid-June sky.

In 1984, art historian Albert Boime argued the painting likely shows the dawn of June 19, with the constellation Aries at its center. Two years later, astronomer Charles Whitney used weather records to rule out the 19th and suggested the sky was actually a composite. With the two theories at odds, the idea that Van Gogh painted real stars faded to what the authors call a “marginal minority view.” Most scholars granted only that the bright point near the horizon was likely Venus.

Kim’s team thought the stars were most likely real, and that the early studies were incomplete. No one had tested the painter’s field of view, the shape of its pattern of stars, and the historical record together. Plus, on the morning of June 19, the Moon was a waning gibbous, past half and nothing like the slim crescent depicted on the canvas.

Rather than assuming a date, the researchers asked whether the sky Van Gogh painted could occur, and when. Their method has two core steps. First, they compare a painted sky with astronomical simulations to see whether its arrangement is even possible. Then, they use a statistical method that measures the similarity between two shapes — called Procrustes analysis — to see how faithfully the painting’s star patterns matched real ones. When more historical data is available, the team also works to reconstruct the artist’s field of view from the landscape and check candidate dates against weather records and letters.

As a proof of concept, they applied the method to a handful of other night paintings. A 2011 study had argued that the stars in German painter Adam Elsheimer’s 1609 The Flight into Egypt weren’t copied from a single real sky, and the team’s test agreed. The painting’s Big Dipper sits at an angle to the Milky Way that never occurs in the night sky.

French painter Jean-François Millet’s Starry Night, painted between 1850 and 1865, has no letters, weather records, or known painting site to draw on, so the team ran only the core astronomical tests. The painting’s depiction of Orion — including the bright star Rigel — and Sirius revealed the tightest fit of any painting in the study to an actual star pattern.

Van Gogh’s own 1888 Starry Night Over the Rhône and Café Terrace at Night were next. Because their painting sites in Arles still stand and his letters and local weather records survive, they got the full treatment. The Big Dipper in Starry Night Over the Rhône matched the real sky with what the authors call “relative precision,” and the Summer Triangle in Café Terrace at Night fit even more closely.

RELATED: How Galileo blended science and art before his death 380 years ago

Then came The Starry Night. Van Gogh is thought to have based the painting’s village on an earlier sketch he had completed of Saint-Rémy. After locating a ridge near the asylum whose view matches the drawing, the team found the sketch captures a zoomed-in slice of the landscape. Measured diagonally, from one corner of the frame to the opposite corner, the field of view spans about 18°. They then made an assumption: that Van Gogh likely framed the painting’s night sky the same way. If he did, there should be a morning on record when the Moon, Venus, and a recognizable star pattern all fit inside that narrow frame and are arranged as painted.

Only three dawns in June and July 1889 put the Moon above Venus, as in the painting, inside that field of view: June 23, July 22, and July 23. Only the July mornings also placed the Hyades in view, and on July 22, the Moon and Venus sat in opposite corners with the cluster in between.

At the center of the canvas, a cluster of stars forms a lopsided V that closely resembles the shape of the Hyades cluster. But any handful of dots can coincidentally look like a V. The team had to evaluate whether these stars were intentionally painted as the Hyades or just happened to resemble the cluster’s shape.

They reasoned that if Van Gogh had painted the real cluster, each painted star should have a real counterpart in the same spot. That is, the star at the point of the painted V should match the star at the point of the real V, and so on down each arm of the cluster. Matching them up that way should give a better fit than any other possible combination. So the team tried every possible way of pairing the five painted stars with the five real ones — 120 combinations in all — and measured how well each fit. The natural, point-to-point pairing was the most accurate.

The match was close, but it wasn’t perfect. Of all the paintings the team tested, The Starry Night fit its stars with the lowest statistical accuracy. The authors also acknowledge that a close shape match alone can’t identify a star group. Some other constellations score as well or better and are ruled out only by other evidence, such as where they sat in the sky that morning. Nevertheless, the combined evidence still suggested July 22 as the most likely date.

One objection to this scenario remained. Historians have long held that a severe seizure in mid-July left Van Gogh unable to work. But after rereading his letters alongside weather records from that summer, the team argues the seizure may have struck later, in the last week of July, leaving Van Gogh free to watch the dawn sky on July 22.

The authors argue that the fact that so many clues converge on one morning makes it “hard to reconcile with the premise that the sky on the canvas is an arbitrary creation.” The simpler explanation is that the painting’s sky is rooted in actual observations of the sky on that morning in July — and the burden of proof now falls on anyone who says Van Gogh invented it.

Because the core test needs nothing but the star positions, the team argues it could be turned on other night paintings, including many no one has yet examined. “I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-Rémy paintings, and at Van Gogh’s movements that summer,” Kim said in a statement. “Our conversation with Van Gogh’s other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one.”

Stellarium, the free planetarium software the team used to cross-check its simulations, lets you simulate the night sky from any place and date. Enter Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, and set the clock to a couple hours before sunrise on July 22, 1889. If the sky looks too bright, turn off the atmosphere in the view settings (or press the keyboard shortcut, A).

Then search for the Hyades cluster. Brilliant Venus sits on one side, a slim crescent Moon slightly higher on the other, and between them the V of the Hyades. You can scroll through the hours to watch the scene wheel up from the horizon before dawn. Then step back a day to July 21, or ahead to July 23 and 24, and watch the Moon slide toward Venus. Or compare the view with June 19, the date Boime proposed, and judge for yourself which sky best fits the canvas.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

#6429. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 5: Smoke out the Southern Cigar

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tonight’s target is a bit of a test: How far south can you see? At a latitude of 40° north, NGC 55 in Sculptor — also called the Southern Cigar Galaxy or the String of Pearls Galaxy — only rises about 10° above the southern horizon at its highest, which occurs around 9 P.M. local time. Observers farther south will see it higher in the sky, while those farther north will see it closer to the horizon or be unable to make it out at all.

For those observers who can catch it, NGC 55 is a bright, 8th-magnitude edge-on barred spiral located just under 4° northwest of magnitude 2.4 Alpha (α) Phoenicis in Phoenix, which sits below the galaxy as you look south around this time of night. This galaxy is not only bright, it’s quite large, stretching roughly the width of the Full Moon (½°) at its longest. It is quite thin, however, only some 6’ wide along the other dimension. You’ll immediately see that its nucleus is not in the center, but offset to the west. Several other bright knots of star formation may also be visible within the galaxy’s plane — particularly if you drop in a nebula filter.
